claim: SATAY allows one-step mapping of all genetic loci in which transposons can insert without disrupting essential functions.
source: SAturated Transposon Analysis in Yeast (SATAY) allows one-step mapping of all genetic loci in which transposons can insert without disrupting essential functions.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the capability of the SATAY method.

claim: SATAY is particularly suited to discover loci important for growth under various conditions.
source: SATAY is particularly suited to discover loci important for growth under various conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key application of the method.

claim: SATAY reveals positive and negative genetic interactions in single and multiple mutant strains.
source: SATAY (1) reveals positive and negative genetic interactions in single and multiple mutant strains
evidence: This is stated as one of the capabilities of SATAY in the abstract.

claim: SATAY can identify drug targets.
source: (2) can identify drug targets
evidence: This is stated as one of the capabilities of SATAY in the abstract.

claim: SATAY detects not only essential genes, but also essential protein domains.
source: (3) detects not only essential genes, but also essential protein domains
evidence: This is stated as one of the capabilities of SATAY in the abstract.

claim: SATAY generates both null and other informative alleles.
source: (4) generates both null and other informative alleles.
evidence: This is stated as one of the capabilities of SATAY in the abstract.

claim: Pib2 (PhosphoInositide-Binding 2) is a master regulator of TORC1.
source: In a SATAY screen for rapamycin-resistant mutants, we identify Pib2 (PhosphoInositide-Binding 2) as a master regulator of TORC1.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Pib2 has two antagonistic TORC1-activating and -inhibiting activities located on opposite ends of the protein.
source: We describe two antagonistic TORC1-activating and -inhibiting activities located on opposite ends of Pib2.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae is an invaluable model for cell biology.
source: Saccharomyces cerevisiae is an invaluable model for cell biology (Weissman, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Despite the simplicity of its genome, yeast's inner working mechanisms are similar to that of higher eukaryotes.
source: Despite the simplicity of its genome, its inner working mechanisms are similar to that of higher eukaryotes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about yeast.

claim: Ordered deletion libraries for every non-essential gene have been generated.
source: Ordered deletion libraries for every non-essential gene have been generated (Giaever et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Ordered libraries of complete deletions only cover non-essential genes.
source: First, ordered libraries of complete deletions only cover non-essential genes.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of ordered deletion libraries.

claim: Deletion strains are prone to accumulate suppressor mutations.
source: Second, deletion strains are prone to accumulate suppressor mutations (Teng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Transposon sequencing (Tn-seq) was developed in various bacterial models.
source: Recently, an innovative approach called Transposon sequencing (Tn-seq) was developed in various bacterial models (Christen et al., 2011; Girgis et al., 2007; van Opijnen et al., 2009)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Transposon sequencing (Tn-seq) was developed in the fungus Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
source: and in the fungus Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Guo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The method utilizes the Maize Ac/Ds transposase/transposon system in yeast.
source: The method utilizes the Maize Ac/Ds transposase/transposon system in yeast (Lazarow et al., 2012; Weil and Kunze, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with citations.

claim: Transposase-induced MiniDs excision is followed by repair of the ADE2 gene with a frequency of ~60%.
source: The excised transposon then re-inserts at random genomic locations with a frequency of ~60% (Lazarow et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and represents a measured frequency.

claim: Seven libraries were generated in ade2Δ strains derived from BY4741 and BY4742 backgrounds.
source: We have generated seven libraries, displayed together in all figures to illustrate the reproducibility of the approach. All libraries were generated in ade2Δ strains derived from BY4741 and BY4742 backgrounds.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental setup.

claim: In wild-type library 1, 284,162 independent transposons could be mapped onto the genome.
source: In this analysis, 284,162 independent transposons could be mapped onto the genome
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the sequencing data analysis.

claim: The average density of transposon insertion is one transposon every 42 bp.
source: representing an average density of one transposon every 42 bp
evidence: This is calculated from the sequencing data.

claim: The median number of reads per transposon is 22.
source: and a median number of 22 reads per transposon.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the sequencing data analysis.

claim: No large area of the genome was devoid of transposon.
source: No large area of the genome was devoid of transposon (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B showing genome-wide transposon distribution.

claim: No strong sequence preference was detected in the insertion sites.
source: Consistent with analyses in Maize (Vollbrecht et al., 2010), no strong sequence preference was detected in the insertion sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Transposon insertion is favored in inter-nucleosomal DNA.
source: Superimposing nucleosome occupancy data (Lee et al., 2007) showed that this was due to favored transposon insertion in inter-nucleosomal DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, Gangadharan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Pericentromeric regions were specifically enriched by ~20% of the transposon insertions.
source: These were the pericentromeric regions (Figure 1B, top), which were specifically enriched by ~20% of the transposon insertions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The transposon map showed that a fraction of the coding DNA sequences (CDS) were devoid of insertions, which coincided almost exactly with genes annotated as essential.
source: The transposon map clearly showed that a fraction of the coding DNA sequences (CDS) were devoid of insertions. These coincided almost exactly with genes annotated as essential (Figure 1C, green arrowheads).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: The median number of transposons inserted in the CDSs of all genes was 18 per gene.
source: The median number of transposons inserted in the CDSs of all genes was 18 per gene (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1D.

claim: The median number of transposons for annotated non-essential genes is 21.
source: This number raised to 21 for annotated non-essential genes
evidence: This is stated in the text as a measurement from the data.

claim: The median number of transposons for annotated essential genes is three.
source: but dropped to three for annotated essential genes (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1E.

claim: SATAY distinguishes, in a single step, genes that are required for growth from those that are not.
source: Thus our method distinguishes, in a single step, genes that are required for growth from those that are not.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing differential transposon coverage in essential vs. non-essential genes.

claim: GAL10 encodes a bifunctional enzyme with an N-terminal epimerase, and a C-terminal mutarotase domain.
source: GAL10 encodes a bifunctional enzyme with an N-terminal epimerase, and a C-terminal mutarotase domain (Majumdar et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The epimerase activity of Gal10 is indispensable in the growth conditions used, while the mutarotase activity is dispensable.
source: While the epimerase activity is indispensable in our conditions, the mutarotase activity is dispensable, as cells were fed a mixture of α- and β-D-Galactose, thus not requiring the conversion of one into the other.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the growth conditions and the observed transposon tolerance pattern.

claim: The junction between the permissive and non-permissive domains of GAL10 corresponds exactly to the junction of the two domains in the Gal10 protein.
source: The junction between the permissive and non-permissive domains of GAL10 corresponds exactly to the junction of the two domains in the Gal10 protein.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the transposon mapping data.

claim: Only the first 76 amino acids of Taf3 are necessary for growth.
source: Our data show that only the first 76 amino acids are necessary for growth.
evidence: This is stated based on the transposon mapping data.

claim: Strains expressing only the first 90 amino acids of Taf3 are viable.
source: Sporulation and progeny segregation confirmed that strains expressing only the first 90 amino acids of Taf3 were viable (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated as a result of genetic validation experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Complete replacement of TAF3 is lethal.
source: By contrast, complete replacement of TAF3 gave rise to only two viable, G418-sensitive spores per meiosis, confirming that TAF3 is essential (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated as a result of genetic validation experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The essential region of Taf3 corresponds to a predicted histone-like bromo-associated domain.
source: The essential region of Taf3 corresponds to a predicted histone-like bromo-associated domain (Doerks et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Only the first 140 amino-acids of Prp45 are necessary for growth.
source: From our data, only the first 140 amino-acids of Prp45 are necessary for growth, which we confirmed using the same strategy as for TAF3 (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is stated based on transposon mapping data and confirmed by genetic validation shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Prp45 is centrally located within the spliceosome, has an extended conformation and makes several contacts with various proteins and snRNAs.
source: Prp45 is centrally located within the spliceosome, has an extended conformation and makes several contacts with various proteins and snRNAs.
evidence: This is stated based on structural data from a cryo-EM structure.

claim: The most conserved region of Prp45 is a loop that makes extensive contacts with U2 and U6 snRNAs close to the active site.
source: In particular, the most conserved region of Prp45 is a loop that makes extensive contacts with U2 and U6 snRNAs close to the active site (Figure 3E–F, yellow).
evidence: This is stated based on structural analysis shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: The most conserved loop of Prp45 belongs to the dispensable part of the protein, suggesting that splicing can occur without it.
source: This loop belongs to the dispensable part of Prp45, surprisingly suggesting that splicing can occur without it.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the transposon mapping data combined with structural information.

claim: SEC9 encodes a SNARE protein.
source: SEC9 encodes a SNARE protein.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the gene.

claim: The essential SNARE domain of Sec9 is located at the C-terminus.
source: The essential SNARE domain, located at the C-terminus (Brennwald et al., 1994), is devoid of transposons.
evidence: This is stated with a citation and supported by transposon mapping data.

claim: The N-terminus of Sec9 is known to be dispensable for growth.
source: The N-terminus of the protein is known to be dispensable for growth (Brennwald et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: ~1200 genes fulfilled the criteria for bearing transposon-tolerant and -intolerant regions.
source: ~1200 genes fulfilled these requirements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated as a result of the algorithm analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 400 best-scoring genes showed clear domain boundaries.
source: of which the 400 best-scoring ones showed clear domain boundaries (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–5).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the algorithm analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2–5.

claim: The gene set with essential subdomains was overwhelmingly enriched for previously-annotated essential genes.
source: Essential subdomains are only expected in essential genes and indeed, this gene set was overwhelmingly enriched for previously-annotated essential genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Single amino-acid substitutions in Vps13 suppress the growth defect of ERMES mutants.
source: We have recently identified single amino-acid substitutions in the endosomal protein Vps13 that suppress the growth defect of mutants of the ER-mitochondria encounter structure (ERMES) (Lang et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Suppression of ERMES mutants by Vps13 is dependent on the proper function of Mcp1.
source: Suppression is dependent on the proper function of the mitochondrial protein Mcp1 (Tan et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Suppression of ERMES mutants by Vps13 is dependent on the proper function of Vam6/Vps39.
source: and on the endosomal protein Vam6/Vps39 (Elbaz-Alon et al., 2014; Hönscher et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: ERMES components fell above the diagonal in the comparison of wild-type and mmm1Δ VPS13(D716H) libraries, indicating they bore more transposons in the mmm1Δ VPS13(D716H) library.
source: Consistent with the ERMES suppressor phenotype of the VPS13(D716H) mutation, ERMES components fell above the diagonal (that is, they bore more transposons in the mmm1Δ VPS13(D716H) than in the wild-type library, Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: VPS13, MCP1 and VAM6/VPS39 fell under the diagonal in the comparison of wild-type and mmm1Δ VPS13(D716H) libraries.
source: By contrast, VPS13, MCP1 and VAM6/VPS39 fell under the diagonal, as expected (Lang et al., 2015a, Figure 4A, C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 4A, C.

claim: Many genes known to display synthetic sick or lethal interaction with mmm1Δ were found, including TOM70, VPS41, YPT7, VMS1 and YME1.
source: Many other genes known to display synthetic sick or lethal interaction with mmm1Δ (Hoppins et al., 2011) were also found, including TOM70, VPS41, YPT7, VMS1 and YME1 (Figure 4A, C).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and supported by data shown in Figure 4A, C.

claim: LCB3 displays synthetic sick interaction with DPL1.
source: LCB3, which displays synthetic sick interaction with DPL1 (Zhang et al., 2001), was less transposon-tolerant in both the dpl1Δ and the dpl1Δ psd2Δ libraries (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PSD1 displays a synthetic lethality with PSD2 on media lacking choline and ethanolamine.
source: By contrast PSD1, which displays a synthetic lethality with PSD2 on media lacking choline and ethanolamine (Birner et al., 2001), was transposon-intolerant in the dpl1Δ psd2Δ library only (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and supported by data shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: VPS13 was less transposon-tolerant in the dpl1Δ psd2Δ library, consistent with a role for Vps13 in interorganelle lipid exchange.
source: Interestingly, we also found that VPS13 was less transposon-tolerant in the dpl1Δ psd2Δ, consistent with a role for Vps13 in interorganelle lipid exchange (AhYoung et al., 2015; Kornmann et al., 2009; Lang et al., 2015a, 2015b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: HIP1 was one of the best hits when comparing the dpl1Δ and wild-type libraries.
source: Additionally, when comparing the dpl1Δ and wild-type libraries, one of the best hits was the histidine permease HIP1 (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: The difference in HIP1 transposon coverage reflects a genetic interaction between HIP1 and HIS3, not between HIP1 and DPL1.
source: This did not, however, reflect a genetic interaction between HIP1 and DPL1, but instead between HIP1 and HIS3; during the construction of the strains, ADE2 was replaced by a HIS3 cassette in the wild-type strain, while it was replaced by a NAT cassette in the dpl1Δ strain.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the observed difference based on the strain construction details.

claim: At low temperature, cdc10Δ cells are viable and able to assemble a septin ring.
source: Indeed, at low temperature, cdc10Δ cells are viable and able to assemble a septin ring.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The Cdc10-less septin ring is based on a Cdc3-Cdc3 interaction, instead of the normal Cdc3-Cdc10 interaction.
source: This Cdc10-less ring is based on a Cdc3-Cdc3 interaction, instead of the normal Cdc3-Cdc10 interaction (McMurray et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The number of transposons mapping within CDC10 increased significantly in the dpl1Δ psd2Δ library, indicating that the absence of Psd2 and Dpl1 suppressed the cdc10Δ phenotype.
source: In the dpl1Δ psd2Δ library, however, the number of transposons mapping within CDC10 increased significantly, indicating that the absence of Psd2 and Dpl1 suppressed the cdc10Δ phenotype (Figure 5A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, bottom left).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dpl1Δ allele alone allowed cdc10Δ cells to grow at higher temperature.
source: Genetic analysis revealed that the dpl1Δ allele alone allowed cdc10Δ cells to grow at higher temperature, indicating that the Cdc10-less septin ring was stabilized in the absence of Dpl1 (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is stated as a result of genetic validation experiments shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The rescue of cdc10Δ by dpl1Δ was independent of PSD2.
source: Genetic analysis also demonstrated that the rescue of cdc10Δ by dpl1Δ was independent of PSD2.
evidence: This is stated as a result of genetic validation experiments.

claim: Dpl1 is an ER protein that does not contact any of the septin subunits.
source: Dpl1 is an ER protein that does not contact any of the septin subunits; its destabilizing effect on the septin ring must therefore be indirect.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the known localization of Dpl1 and the septin ring.

claim: The stabilizing effect of low temperature on Cdc10-less septin rings might be the result of changes in plasma membrane properties, which can be mimicked by DPL1 ablation.
source: Thus, the stabilizing effect of low temperature on Cdc10-less septin rings might not only be the result of a direct stabilization of Cdc3-Cdc3 interaction, but also of changes in plasma membrane properties, which can be mimicked by DPL1 ablation.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the observed data and known properties of Dpl1 and membranes.

claim: Yen1 is a member of the Xeroderma Pigmentosum G (XPG) family of 5'-flap endonucleases.
source: a library made from a strain expressing a constitutively active version of the Holliday-junction resolvase Yen1, a member of the Xeroderma Pigmentosum G (XPG) family of 5'-flap endonucleases (Ip et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: In wild-type strains, Yen1 is kept inactive during the S-phase of the cell cycle via Cdk-mediated phosphorylation.
source: In wild-type strains, Yen1 is kept inactive during the S-phase of the cell cycle via Cdk-mediated phosphorylation (Matos et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: When nine Cdk1 target sites are mutated to alanine, Yen1 becomes refractory to inhibitory phosphorylation and active during S-phase.
source: When nine Cdk1 target sites are mutated to alanine, Yen1 becomes refractory to inhibitory phosphorylation and active during S-phase (Yen1on) (Blanco et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Under YEN1on conditions, the essential gene DNA2 became tolerant to transposon insertion.
source: We discovered that, under these conditions, the essential gene DNA2 became tolerant to transposon insertion (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The presence of the YEN1on allele led to a rescue of the lethal phenotype of dna2Δ strains.
source: Further genetic analyses confirmed that the presence of the YEN1on allele led to a rescue of the lethal phenotype of dna2Δ strains; spores bearing the dna2 deletion failed to grow unless they additionally bore the YEN1on allele (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated as a result of genetic validation experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: At 25°C, the colony size of dna2Δ YEN1on spores was comparable to that of the DNA2 counterparts.
source: Moreover, at 25°C, the colony size of dna2Δ YEN1on spores was comparable to that of the DNA2 counterparts (Figure 5E, right).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: dna2Δ YEN1on cells accumulated in S- and G2-phases.
source: However, FACS analysis of DNA content revealed that dna2Δ YEN1on cells accumulated in S- and G2-phases (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated as a result of FACS analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: DNA2 encodes a large protein with both helicase and endonuclease activities.
source: DNA2 encodes a large protein with both helicase and endonuclease activities (Budd and Campbell, 1995).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: While the helicase activity of Dna2 can be disrupted without affecting yeast viability, the nuclease activity is essential.
source: Interestingly, while the helicase activity can be disrupted without affecting yeast viability, the nuclease activity is essential (Ölmezer et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Yen1 is able to partially fulfill the essential roles of Dna2, provided that its activity is unrestrained in S-phase.
source: Our genetic data now reveal that Yen1 is able to partially fulfill the essential roles of Dna2, provided that its activity is unrestrained in S-phase.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic data.

claim: Yen1on may be able to substitute the essential function of Dna2 by providing 5'-flap nuclease activity in S-phase.
source: Since the spectrum of Yen1 substrates includes 5'-flap structures (Ip et al., 2008), Yen1on may be able to substitute the essential function of Dna2 by providing 5'-flap nuclease activity in S-phase.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the known substrate specificity of Yen1 and the observed genetic data.

claim: Yen1 serves as a backup for the resolution of replication intermediates that arise in helicase-defective mutants of Dna2.
source: This finding extends previous work showing that Yen1 serves as a backup for the resolution of replication intermediates that arise in helicase-defective mutants of Dna2 (Ölmezer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Rapamycin blocks cell proliferation by inhibiting TORC1, through binding to Fpr1.
source: Rapamycin blocks cell proliferation by inhibiting the target of rapamycin complex I (TORC1), through binding to the Fk506-sensitive Proline Rotamase Fpr1 (Heitman et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The TORC1 complex integrates nutrient-sensing pathways and regulates cellular growth accordingly.
source: The TORC1 complex integrates nutrient-sensing pathways and regulates cellular growth accordingly.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TORC1.

claim: FPR1 was the best hit in the rapamycin-treated library.
source: Expectedly, the best hit was FPR1, encoding the receptor for rapamycin (Hall, 1996).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data with a citation.

claim: Other hits in the rapamycin-treated library included RRD1, TIP41, GLN3, SAP190, PSP2, CCS1, ESL2 and members of the PP2A phosphatase PPH21 and PPM1.
source: Other hits included RRD1 (Rapamycin-Resistant Deletion 1), TIP41, GLN3, SAP190, PSP2, CCS1, ESL2 and members of the PP2A phosphatase PPH21 and PPM1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: These genes are either directly involved in rapamycin signaling or known to confer rapamycin resistance upon deletion.
source: These genes are either directly involved in rapamycin signaling or known to confer rapamycin resistance upon deletion (Xie et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: PIB2 deletion confers sensitivity, not resistance, to rapamycin.
source: Finding the TORC1 regulator PIB2 (Kim and Cunningham, 2015) was however unexpected, because PIB2 deletion confers sensitivity, not resistance, to rapamycin (Kim and Cunningham, 2015; Parsons et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: All the insertions selected by rapamycin treatment mapped to the 5'-end of PIB2.
source: All the insertions selected by rapamycin treatment mapped to the 5'-end of the gene (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The rest of PIB2 was less covered in the rapamycin-treated than in non-rapamycin-treated libraries.
source: On the contrary, the rest of PIB2 was less covered in the rapamycin-treated than in non-rapamycin-treated libraries (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Insertions in the 5' end of PIB2 conferred rapamycin resistance, while insertions elsewhere conferred rapamycin sensitivity.
source: Insertions in the 5' end of PIB2 therefore conferred rapamycin resistance, while insertions elsewhere, like complete deletion of PIB2, conferred rapamycin sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the transposon mapping data.

claim: Strains expressing Pib2 variants that were truncated from the first until up to amino acid 304 were hyperresistant to rapamycin.
source: Strains expressing Pib2 variants that were truncated from the first until up to amino acid 304 were hyperresistant to rapamycin (Figure 6C, top).
evidence: This is stated as a result of genetic validation experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Complete PIB2 deletion caused rapamycin hypersensitivity.
source: We also confirmed that, by contrast, complete PIB2 deletion caused rapamycin hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is stated as a result of genetic validation experiments.

claim: A larger N-terminal truncation of Pib2 extending beyond the mapped territory of rapamycin resistance-conferring transposons did not mediate hyperresistance to rapamycin.
source: A larger N-terminal truncation extending beyond the mapped territory of rapamycin resistance-conferring transposons, did not mediate hyperresistance to rapamycin (Figure 6G, Pib2426-635).
evidence: This is stated as a result of genetic validation experiments shown in Figure 6G.

claim: When Pib2165-635 and full-length Pib2 were co-expressed, the rapamycin hyperresistance was mitigated, indicating that the effect of the truncated Pib2 protein was semi-dominant.
source: In these conditions, the rapamycin hyperresistance was mitigated, indicating that the effect of the truncated Pib2 protein was semi-dominant (Figure 6C, bottom).
evidence: This is stated as a result of genetic validation experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Expressing the Pib2 truncation from a high-copy (2 µ) vector did not further increase resistance to rapamycin.
source: Expressing the truncation from a high-copy (2 µ) vector did not further increase resistance to rapamycin, indicating that higher expression levels did not change the semi-dominance of the PIB2 truncation allele.
evidence: This is stated as a result of genetic validation experiments.

claim: Pib2 positively regulates TORC1 function.
source: Because gain-of-function alleles of PIB2 lead to rapamycin resistance, while loss-of-function alleles lead to sensitivity, our data suggest that Pib2 positively regulates TORC1 function.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic data.

claim: Pib2 deficiency severely blunted TORC1 activation following glutamine addition to proline-grown cells.
source: Pib2 deficiency severely blunted TORC1 activation in these conditions (Figure 6D, top).
evidence: This is stated as a result of TORC1 activation assays shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A strain lacking GTR1 showed a similarly blunted response with respect to TORC1 activation following glutamine addition to proline-grown cells.
source: In a control experiment, a strain lacking GTR1 – a component of the TORC1-activating EGO (Exit from rapamycin-induced GrOwth arrest) complex, which is orthologous to the mammalian Rag GTPase-Ragulator complex (Chantranupong et al., 2015; Powis and De Virgilio, 2016) – showed a similarly blunted response with respect to TORC1 activation following glutamine addition to proline-grown cells (Figure 6D, top).
evidence: This is stated as a result of TORC1 activation assays shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Glutamine-mediated TORC1 activation appeared normal in a strain expressing an N-terminally truncated Pib2 variant (pPIB2165-635).
source: By contrast, glutamine-mediated TORC1 activation appeared normal in a strain expressing an N-terminally truncated Pib2 variant (pPIB2165-635, Figure 6D, bottom).
evidence: This is stated as a result of TORC1 activation assays shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Like Gtr1, Pib2 is necessary to activate TORC1 in response to amino acids.
source: Thus, like Gtr1, Pib2 is necessary to activate TORC1 in response to amino acids.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the TORC1 activation assays.

claim: The N-terminus of Pib2 appears to be an inhibitory domain.
source: The N-terminus of Pib2 appears to be an inhibitory domain.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic and biochemical data.

claim: The ablation of the N-terminal inhibitory domain of Pib2 confers rapamycin resistance, yet is not sufficient to constitutively activate TORC1.
source: The ablation of this domain confers rapamycin resistance, yet is not sufficient to constitutively activate TORC1 (e.g. in proline-grown cells).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic and biochemical data.

claim: Pib2 harbored at least two central Kog1-binding regions.
source: We found that Pib2 harbored at least two central Kog1-binding regions, since two mostly non-overlapping fragments (Pib21-312 and Pib2304-635) showed robust interaction with Kog1 (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a result of yeast-two-hybrid assays shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Kog1 binding is not essential for Pib2-mediated TORC1 activation.
source: Kog1 binding is, however, not essential for Pib2-mediated TORC1 activation, since cells expressing a fragment without these Kog1-binding domains (Pib2426-635) were as rapamycin-resistant as cells expressing full length Pib2 (FL, Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Pib2 truncations lacking the FYVE domain are unable to bind PI3P, and hence to properly localize to the vacuole.
source: Pib2 truncations lacking the FYVE domain are unable to bind PI3P, and hence to properly localize to the vacuole (Kim and Cunningham, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: When cells expressed FYVE domain-truncated Pib2 (Pib2Δ426-532), their rapamycin resistance decreased, but not as severely as observed in pib2Δ strains.
source: When cells expressed FYVE domain-truncated Pib2 (Pib2Δ426-532), their rapamycin resistance decreased, but not as severely as observed in pib2Δ strains (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated as a result of genetic validation experiments shown in Figure 6G.

claim: FYVE-domain-mediated vacuolar recruitment is not absolutely required for Pib2 to activate TORC1.
source: This indicates that FYVE-domain-mediated vacuolar recruitment is not absolutely required for Pib2 to activate TORC1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic data.

claim: Cells expressing Pib2 variants that were either truncated at the extreme C-terminus (PIB21-620) or carried a deletion within the C-terminus (PIB2∆533-620) were as sensitive to rapamycin as pib2∆ cells.
source: Strikingly, cells expressing Pib2 variants that were either truncated at the extreme C-terminus (PIB21-620) or carried a deletion within the C-terminus (PIB2∆533-620) were as sensitive to rapamycin as pib2∆ cells (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated as a result of genetic validation experiments shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The C-terminus of Pib2 is important to ensure proper TORC1 activation.
source: The C-terminus of Pib2 is therefore important to ensure proper TORC1 activation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic data.

claim: Pib2 harbors a large N-terminal Inhibitory Domain (NID), and a C-terminal TORC1-Activating Domain (CAD).
source: We conclude that Pib2 harbors the following functional domains: a large N-terminal Inhibitory Domain (NID), and a C-terminal TORC1-Activating Domain (CAD)
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic and biochemical data.

claim: The central portion of Pib2 harbors FYVE and Kog1-binding domains for proper targeting of Pib2 to the vacuole and TORC1, respectively.
source: the central portion of the protein harbors FYVE and Kog1-binding domains for proper targeting of Pib2 to the vacuole and TORC1, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic and biochemical data.

claim: The NID activity of the endogenously-expressed wild-type Pib2 is able to mitigate the rapamycin resistance conferred by ectopic expression of the CAD.
source: Thus, the NID activity of the endogenously-expressed wild-type Pib2 is able to mitigate the rapamycin resistance conferred by ectopic expression (or overexpression) of the CAD.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic data.

claim: The NID does not auto-inhibit the CAD within Pib2, but rather, the NID and CAD act independently and antagonistically on TORC1.
source: Therefore, our data suggest that the NID does not auto-inhibit the CAD within Pib2, but rather, that the NID and CAD act independently and antagonistically on TORC1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic data.

claim: Expressing CAD-truncated Pib2 should semi-dominantly inhibit TORC1.
source: This latter scenario predicts that, just as expressing NID-truncated Pib2 semi-dominantly activates TORC1 (Figure 6C), expressing CAD-truncated Pib2 should semi-dominantly inhibit it.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on the model of independent NID and CAD activities.

claim: Strains expressing the two CAD truncations Pib2Δ533-620 and Pib21-620 in an otherwise wild-type background were significantly more sensitive to rapamycin than their counterparts expressing only full length Pib2.
source: To test this prediction, we expressed the two CAD truncations Pib2Δ533-620 and Pib21-620 in an otherwise wild-type strain. The resulting strains were significantly more sensitive to rapamycin than their counterparts expressing only full length Pib2 (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is stated as a result of genetic validation experiments shown in Figure 6H.

claim: When pib2Δ cells expressed the Pib2 CAD truncation alleles, they became even more sensitive to rapamycin.
source: Furthermore, when pib2Δ cells expressed the Pib2 CAD truncation alleles, they became even more sensitive to rapamycin.
evidence: This is stated as a result of genetic validation experiments.

claim: Pib2-NID does not act in an auto-inhibitory manner, but rather inhibits TORC1 independently of the presence of a Pib2-CAD.
source: Therefore, Pib2-NID does not act in an auto-inhibitory manner, but rather inhibits TORC1 independently of the presence of a Pib2-CAD.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic data.

claim: Pib2-NID does not inhibit TORC1 by antagonizing Gtr1-Gtr2.
source: This does not appear to be the case; first, the expression of Pib2Δ533-620 or Pib21-620 further enhanced the rapamycin sensitivity of gtr1Δ gtr2Δ cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), and second, the Pib2Δ533-620- or Pib21-620-mediated rapamycin hypersensitivity was not suppressed by expression of the constitutively active, TORC1-activating Gtr1Q65L-Gtr2S23L module (Binda et al., 2009; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Pib2-NID inhibits TORC1 independently of the EGO complex.
source: These results suggest that Pib2-NID inhibits TORC1 independently of the EGO complex.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic data.

claim: Pib2 is targeted to TORC1 by binding to the vacuolar membrane through its FYVE domain and to Kog1 via its middle portion.
source: In summary, Pib2 is targeted to TORC1 by binding to the vacuolar membrane through its FYVE domain and to Kog1 via its middle portion.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings.

claim: Both repressing and activating activities of Pib2 influence TORC1 independently and do not appear to compete for the same sites on TORC1.
source: The dose-independent semi-dominant nature of the respective truncations indicates that both repressing and activating activities influence TORC1 independently and do not appear to compete for the same sites on TORC1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic data.

claim: High-quality amino acids, such as glutamine, balance the antagonistic TORC1-activating and -repressing activities of Pib2 to tune growth rate according to available resources.
source: We speculate that high-quality amino acids, such as glutamine, balance the antagonistic TORC1-activating and -repressing activities of Pib2 to tune growth rate according to available resources.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the findings.

claim: SATAY can reveal positive and negative genetic interactions, auxotrophies, drug-sensitive or -resistant mutants, and map functional protein domains.
source: SAturated Transposon Analysis in Yeast (SATAY) can reveal positive and negative genetic interactions, auxotrophies, drug-sensitive or -resistant mutants, and map functional protein domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the method's capabilities.

claim: SATAY combines advantages from both classical genetics and high-throughput robotic screens.
source: SATAY combines advantages from both classical genetics and high-throughput robotic screens.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a characterization of the method.

claim: SATAY can in principle be implemented in any strain background, since it does not rely on the existence of available deletion libraries and does not necessitate markers to follow genetic traits.
source: SATAY can in principle be implemented in any strain background, since it does not rely on the existence of available deletion libraries and does not necessitate markers to follow genetic traits.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of the method.

claim: SATAY explores a wide genetic space; exotic alleles can be generated as exemplified by PIB2.
source: Moreover, SATAY explores a wide genetic space; exotic alleles can be generated as exemplified by PIB2 (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), where transposon insertions in different regions of the gene generate opposite phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to the PIB2 example.

claim: Transposon insertion is not limited to CDSs; promoters of essential genes are often transposon-intolerant.
source: Transposon insertion is not limited to CDSs; we observe that promoters of essential genes are often transposon-intolerant (Figure 2, see GAL10, SGV1, MMS21, RET2, HRR25, NPA3, SEC9, SWI1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Known essential tRNA, snRNA, as well as SRP RNA genes are transposon intolerant.
source: We also observe that known essential tRNA, snRNA, as well as SRP RNA genes are transposon intolerant (see Supplementary Dataset).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to the Supplementary Dataset.

claim: SATAY data reveal transposon-intolerant areas of the genome that do not correspond to any annotated feature, indicating that SATAY could help discover yet-unknown functional elements.
source: Finally, our data reveal transposon-intolerant areas of the genome that do not correspond to any annotated feature, indicating that SATAY could help discover yet-unknown functional elements.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a potential application of the method.

claim: SATAY yields unprecedented insight on the domain structure-function relationship of important proteins, and allows the mapping of important functional domains, without prior knowledge.
source: SATAY yields unprecedented insight on the domain structure-function relationship of important proteins, and allows the mapping of important functional domains, without prior knowledge.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a key advantage of the method.

claim: Dispensable domains in essential proteins might not be required for the essential function of these proteins, but may have other roles.
source: Dispensable domains in essential proteins might not be required for the essential function of these proteins, but may have other roles.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The sub-gene resolution enabled by SATAY may unveil yet-unsuspected accessory or regulatory functions, even in otherwise well-studied proteins.
source: The sub-gene resolution enabled by SATAY may thus unveil yet-unsuspected accessory or regulatory functions, even in otherwise well-studied proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a potential application of the method.

claim: Structure-function information revealed by SATAY may guide 3D-structure determination efforts by indicating possibly flexible accessory domains.
source: In addition, structure-function information revealed by SATAY may guide 3D-structure determination efforts by indicating possibly flexible accessory domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a potential application of the method.

claim: The resolution of a SATAY screen is directly proportional to the number of transposons mapped onto the genome.
source: The resolution of a SATAY screen is directly proportional to the number of transposons mapped onto the genome.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a characteristic of the method.

claim: The current resolution of SATAY is ~1/40 bp, which is amply sufficient to confidently identify essential genes and protein domains.
source: The current resolution is ~1/40 bp, which is amply sufficient to confidently identify essential genes and protein domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a characterization of the method's performance.

claim: Not every colony generates a detectable transposon due to several reasons including that excised transposons only reinsert in 60% of the cases.
source: Not every colony generates a detectable transposon. This is due to several reasons. (1) Excised transposons only reinsert in 60% of the cases (our observations and Lazarow et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: 7% of the sequencing reads mapped onto repetitive DNA elements and were discarded because of ambiguous mapping.
source: (2) 7% of the sequencing reads mapped onto repetitive DNA elements (such as rDNA, Ty-elements and subtelomeric repeats) and were discarded because of ambiguous mapping.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a reason for not detecting all transposons.

claim: Increasing both the size of the original library and the sequencing depth leads to an increase in mapped transposon number.
source: We observe that increasing both the size of the original library and the sequencing depth leads to an increase in mapped transposon number (albeit non-proportional, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to Table 1.

claim: The resolution of a SATAY screen can be tailored according to the question and the available resource.
source: Therefore, the resolution of a screen can be tailored according to the question and the available resource.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a characteristic of the method.

claim: SATAY can be utilized to probe, not only the function of the genome, but also its physical and regulatory features, such as nucleosome position and 3D architecture.
source: Thus, SATAY can be utilized to probe, not only the function of the genome, but also its physical and regulatory features, such as nucleosome position and 3D architecture.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a potential application of the method.

claim: SATAY does not require any particular equipment besides access to a sequencing platform, and involves a limited amount of work.
source: Finally, SATAY does not require any particular equipment besides access to a sequencing platform, and involves a limited amount of work.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of the method.

claim: SATAY can be easily multiplexed to perform several genome-wide screens simultaneously.
source: It can be easily multiplexed to perform several genome-wide screens simultaneously.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of the method.

claim: Each SATAY screen yields two measures: the number of transposons and the number of sequencing reads, both of which, for each gene, reveal the fitness of the cognate mutant.
source: Each screen yields two measures, the number of transposons and the number of sequencing reads, both of which, for each gene, reveal the fitness of the cognate mutant.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a characteristic of the method.

claim: The number of transposons per gene is appropriate to look for genes that become important for growth, as in genetic interaction screens.
source: While the number of transposons per gene is appropriate to look for genes that become important for growth, as in genetic interaction screens
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as guidance on how to use the method.

claim: The number of sequencing reads is better suited to identify strains that are positively selected, like drug-resistant mutants.
source: the number of sequencing reads is better suited to identify strains that are positively selected, like drug-resistant mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as guidance on how to use the method.

claim: Noise in SATAY data can be reduced by comparing multiple libraries against each other.
source: We show that this noise can be reduced by comparing multiple libraries against each other (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Comparing multiple libraries allows to tailor the composition of each library set to needs.
source: Moreover, comparing multiple libraries allows to tailor the composition of each library set to needs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of the method.

claim: Increasing the number of libraries will likely decrease the incidence of false positive and false negative in genetic interaction detection.
source: Thus, while signal-to-noise ratio might be a limiting factor for the detection of genetic interactions, we anticipate that increasing the number of libraries, for instance by generating multiple libraries in each condition, will likely decrease the incidence of false positive and false negative.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a prediction about improving the method.

claim: With the increasing number of screens performed in various conditions will come the ability to find correlation patterns among genes that are required or dispensable for growth in similar sets of conditions.
source: With the increasing number of screens performed in various conditions will also come the ability to find correlation patterns among genes that are required or dispensable for growth in similar sets of conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a prediction about future applications of the method.

claim: Such correlations are accurate predictors of common functions and have been extensively used in synthetic genetic screens, such as the E-MAP procedure.
source: Such correlations are accurate predictors of common functions and have been extensively used in synthetic genetic screens, such as the E-MAP procedure (Kornmann et al., 2009; Schuldiner et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: While E-MAP screens compute patterns of genetic interaction on a subset of chosen genetic interaction partners, SATAY allows to detect genetic interactions at the genome scale.
source: However, while E-MAP screens compute patterns of genetic interaction on a subset of chosen genetic interaction partners, SATAY allows to detect genetic interactions at the genome scale.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a comparison between methods.

claim: The approach should be amenable to other industrially-, medically- or scientifically-relevant haploid fungi, such as Y. lipolytica, C. glabrata, K. lactis and P. pastoris.
source: Because the approach only necessitates a transposon and a transposase, it should not only be feasible in S. cerevisiae and S. pombe (Guo et al., 2013), but also amenable to other industrially-, medically- or scientifically-relevant haploid fungi, such as Y. lipolytica, C. glabrata, K. lactis and P. pastoris.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a prediction about the applicability of the method.

claim: The Ds transposon can in principle accommodate extra sequences with no known length limitation.
source: The Ds transposon can in principle accommodate extra sequences with no known length limitation (Lazarow et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Improved designs of the transposon will not only permit finer mapping of protein domains without reliance on spurious transcription and translation, but might allow the exploration of an even wider genetic space.
source: Improved designs will not only permit finer mapping of protein domains without reliance on spurious transcription and translation, but might allow the exploration of an even wider genetic space, for instance by generating gain-of-function variants, thus enabling the development of novel approaches to interrogate the yeast genome.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a prediction about future developments of the method.

claim: Typically 7,000–10,000 colonies with a narrow size distribution can be generated on a 8.4 cm-Ø petri dish.
source: Typically 7,000–10,000 colonies with a narrow size distribution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) can be generated on a 8.4 cm-Ø petri dish.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the case of wild-type library 1, 240 plates yielded ~1.6E6 clones.
source: In the case of wild-type library 1, 240 plates yielded ~1.6E6 clones (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with reference to Table 1.

claim: 500 mg cell pellet should yield 20–60 μg DNA.
source: 500 mg cell pellet should yield 20–60 μg DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as an expected yield.
